Representational Atoms in Neural Networks

Chenhui Hu Affiliation: The Key Laboratory of Cognition and Decision Intelligence for Complex Systems,
Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence,

Abstract

Understanding the internal representations of neural networks and characterizing their relationship with human conceptual structure are two critical questions for elucidating model mechanisms. The former reveals how learned knowledge is organized in internal representations, whereas the latter provides a basis for interpreting these representations through human conceptual structure. Here, we formally define fundamental representational units (FRUs) and establish two evaluation criteria: fidelity and stability. We further prove that threshold-activated sparse autoencoders (TSAEs) can identify FRUs with high fidelity and stability under appropriate conditions, and validate this result through large-scale experiments. Further analyses reveal that FRUs with higher stability exhibit greater monosemanticity and can be composed across layers to recover semantic organization corresponding to human conceptual structure. These results provide a unified framework for defining, evaluating and identifying FRUs in neural networks, and establish a foundation for characterizing the relationship between neural network representations and human conceptual structure.

Neural networks progressively form internal representations during forward propagation, encoding input-related information that supports subsequent prediction or generation LeCun et al. (2015); Bengio et al. (2013). However, how these representations encode and organize the information learned by the model remains incompletely understood Bau et al. (2020); Klindt et al. (2026). A fundamental question is whether this representational organization can be understood in terms of basic units that can be rigorously defined and reliably identified. If so, these units would provide a natural basis for characterizing the semantic organization of internal representations, raising a further question of whether and how this organization relates to human conceptual structure. Addressing these questions is essential for understanding neural representations and their relationship with human conceptual structure.

To answer the first question, we develop a theoretical framework for defining, evaluating and identifying fundamental representational units (FRUs) underlying internal representations. Drawing on compressed sensing Donoho (2006); Candès et al. (2006), we formulate internal representations as sparse linear combinations of FRUs: linearity provides a simple and analytically tractable form for characterizing how these FRUs combine, while sparsity permits them to remain distinguishable under appropriate conditions. On this basis, we formally define the FRUs as representational atoms, or atoms for brevity. This definition operates at the level of internal representation spaces and does not depend on particular neural network architectures.

Within this framework, we next evaluate how closely candidate representational units conform to the definition of representational atoms. Specifically, we introduce two evaluation criteria, fidelity and stability. Fidelity measures how well candidate FRUs reconstruct the original representations, whereas stability measures whether distinct candidate FRUs remain distinguishable from one another. We further establish that the distinguishability captured by stability is a prerequisite for monosemanticity, that is, for each FRU to support a unique semantic interpretation. These criteria enable two widely studied representational units, neurons and learned features Chen et al. (2025a); Huben et al. (2024); Bricken et al. (2023); Templeton et al. (2024), to be quantitatively compared as candidate FRUs within a unified framework. Our experiments show that neurons generally exhibit high fidelity but low stability, whereas learned features exhibit higher stability but lower fidelity. This contrast is consistent with previous observations that learned features tend to be more monosemantic than individual neurons Elhage et al. (2022); Chen et al. (2025b); Bricken et al. (2023); Templeton et al. (2024).

The limitations of existing candidate FRUs raises a critical question: what kind of representation learning mechanism can reliably identify atoms with both high fidelity and stability? To address this question, we prove that threshold-activated sparse autoencoders (TSAEs) can effectively identify representational atoms under appropriate conditions. In practice, we instantiate TSAEs as BiJumpReLU SAEs and evaluate them on internal representations from diverse pretrained neural networks spanning different architectures and representation modalities. Across these settings, BiJumpReLU SAEs consistently identify atoms with high fidelity and stability, outperforming representative SAE variants spanning different activation and sparsity mechanisms Huben et al. (2024); Gao et al. (2025); Zhu et al. (2026); Rajamanoharan et al. (2024b). These large-scale experiments support our theoretical results and establish a practical basis for identifying and analyzing FRUs in neural networks. We further examine whether the theoretical connection between stability and monosemanticity is reflected empirically and find a significant positive correlation between the two, with more stable atoms exhibiting clearer and more consistent semantics.

We finally examine whether and how representational atoms relate to human conceptual structure using HowNet Dong and Dong (2003); Qi et al. (2019), an expert-annotated knowledge base that represents concepts in terms of fine-grained semantic primitives known as sememes. We find that their relationship is not one-to-one: although a small subset of atoms directly aligns with complete sememes, individual sememes are more commonly represented in a distributed manner by multiple atoms from different layers. These findings indicate that representational atoms function as finer-grained semantic components that can be composed into higher-order structures corresponding to human conceptual organization. Notably, their compositions recover not only sememe structures with substantially greater alignment than single atoms but also additional semantic structures that, upon manual verification, are consistent with the corresponding sememes yet not captured by their HowNet annotations. Overall, our work integrates the definition, evaluation and identification of FRUs with the analysis of their semantic and compositional organization, providing a systematic characterization of neural representational structure and its relationship with human conceptual structure.

Results

In the following, we first formally define FRUs and introduce fidelity and stability as two evaluation criteria. We then quantitatively compare neurons and learned features as candidate FRUs within this unified framework. Next, we prove that TSAEs can effectively identify representational atoms under appropriate conditions and validate their practical effectiveness through large-scale experiments. We further examine the relationship between stability and monosemanticity, and finally use HowNet to characterize the relationship between neural representations and human conceptual structure.

Representational atoms

Neurons and learned features are two widely studied candidates for the basic units of internal representations Chen et al. (2025a); Huben et al. (2024); Bricken et al. (2023); Templeton et al. (2024), yet neither provides a principled basis for determining what properties representational components must possess to qualify as FRUs. We therefore begin by formalizing this problem and developing a principled definition of FRUs.

Given a set of high-dimensional internal representations M={𝒎i∣𝒎i∈ℝH}i=1|M|M=\{\boldsymbol{m}_{i}\mid\boldsymbol{m}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{H}\}_{i=1}^{|M|}, we seek a set of FRUs D={𝒅j∣𝒅j∈ℝH}j=1|D|D=\{\boldsymbol{d}_{j}\mid\boldsymbol{d}_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{H}\}_{j=1}^{|D|}. A natural starting point is the standard orthonormal basis of the representation space, treating the coordinate directions (i.e. neurons) as candidate FRUs. However, this choice has two limitations. First, individual coordinate directions need not support stable and well-defined semantics, consistent with the widespread polysemanticity of individual neurons Elhage et al. (2022); Bricken et al. (2023); Templeton et al. (2024). Second, orthogonality restricts the number of candidate FRUs to the dimensionality of the representation space, limiting their ability to capture richer representational structure.

The key property of the standard orthonormal basis is that orthogonality makes distinct coordinate directions and their combinations unambiguously distinguishable, which ensures a unique decomposition of each representation. However, a key insight here is that orthogonality is not necessary for distinguishability. In particular, compressed sensing shows that sparsity can preserve the distinguishability among non-orthogonal components under appropriate conditions Donoho (2006); Candès et al. (2006), which we specify below. We therefore model each internal representation as a sparse linear combination

∀i∈[|M|],𝒎i=𝑫​𝜹i,‖𝜹i‖0≤K,\forall i\in[|M|],\quad\boldsymbol{m}_{i}=\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{\delta}_{i},\qquad\|\boldsymbol{\delta}_{i}\|_{0}\leq K, (1)

where [|M|]={1,2,…,|M|}[|M|]=\{1,2,\ldots,|M|\}, 𝑫=[𝒅1𝒅2⋯𝒅|D|]∈ℝH×|D|\boldsymbol{D}=[\boldsymbol{d}_{1}\ \boldsymbol{d}_{2}\ \cdots\ \boldsymbol{d}_{|D|}]\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times|D|} denotes the dictionary of candidate FRUs, 𝜹i∈ℝ|D|\boldsymbol{\delta}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{|D|} is the sparse coefficient vector associated with 𝒎i\boldsymbol{m}_{i}, ∥⋅∥0\|\cdot\|_{0} denotes the number of non-zero entries, and K∈ℕ+K\in\mathbb{N}^{+} is an upper bound on the sparsity level.

Candidate FRUs that satisfy the distinguishability condition derived below are termed representational atoms, or simply atoms (Fig. 1a). Characterizing this condition in the non-orthogonal setting requires an inner product that captures the relative geometry among candidate FRUs. The standard Euclidean inner product, ⟨𝒅i,𝒅j⟩=𝒅i⊤​𝒅j\langle\boldsymbol{d}_{i},\boldsymbol{d}_{j}\rangle=\boldsymbol{d}_{i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{d}_{j}, characterizes geometry in the ambient representation space, but does not fully capture the geometry induced by internal representations (see ‘Representational atoms theoretical framework’ in Methods). We therefore introduce the atomic inner product (AIP), ⟨𝒅i,𝒅j⟩S~=𝒅i⊤​S~​𝒅j\langle\boldsymbol{d}_{i},\boldsymbol{d}_{j}\rangle_{\tilde{S}}=\boldsymbol{d}_{i}^{\top}\tilde{S}\boldsymbol{d}_{j}, where S~\tilde{S} denotes the representation-induced metric, to characterize their relative geometry (see ‘Atomic inner product’ in Methods). Empirical analyses further show that the AIP better captures the geometry relevant to representational distinguishability (see ‘Empirical validation of the atomic inner product’ section in Supplementary Information).

Using the AIP, we derive a condition under which candidate FRUs remain distinguishable in the non-orthogonal setting. Specifically, extending the classical coherence-based condition Donoho and Elad (2003); Tropp (2004), we prove that, for a KK-sparse representation, distinguishability is preserved when μ<12​K−1\mu<\frac{1}{2K-1}, where μ=maxi≠j⁡|⟨𝒅i,𝒅j⟩S~|\mu=\max_{i\neq j}\left|\langle\boldsymbol{d}_{i},\boldsymbol{d}_{j}\rangle_{\tilde{S}}\right| denotes the maximum coherence among candidate FRUs (see ‘Evaluation of atoms’ in Methods). Within this regime, distinct units and their compositions remain distinguishable from alternative units or compositions, a property we term monorepresentationality. Monorepresentationality constitutes a necessary structural condition for monosemanticity, as each representational unit can support a unique semantic interpretation only when it remains distinguishable from alternative units or compositions. See ‘Evaluation of atoms’ in Methods for the formal definition and discussion of monorepresentationality.

To quantitatively assess how closely candidate FRUs conform to the properties of representational atoms, we introduce two complementary metrics, fidelity and stability (Fig. 1b). Fidelity measures how well candidate FRUs reconstruct the original internal representations and is quantified by the coefficient of determination

R2:=1−∑i‖𝒎i−𝒎^i‖22∑i‖𝒎i−𝒎¯‖22,R^{2}:=1-\frac{\sum_{i}\|\boldsymbol{m}_{i}-\hat{\boldsymbol{m}}_{i}\|_{2}^{2}}{\sum_{i}\|\boldsymbol{m}_{i}-\bar{\boldsymbol{m}}\|_{2}^{2}}, (2)

where 𝒎^i\hat{\boldsymbol{m}}_{i} denotes the reconstructed representation and 𝒎¯\bar{\boldsymbol{m}} denotes the mean of the internal representations (see ‘Fidelity metrics and computation’ in Methods). Stability measures the extent to which candidate FRUs satisfy the distinguishability condition and is quantified by the maximum quantile

q∗:=sup{q∣μq<12​Kq−1},q^{*}:=\sup\left\{q\mid\mu_{q}<\frac{1}{2K_{q}-1}\right\}, (3)

where μq\mu_{q} and KqK_{q} denote the coherence and sparsity level at quantile qq, respectively (see ‘Stability metrics and computation’ in Methods). Ideal representational atoms achieve R2=1R^{2}=1 and q∗=1q^{*}=1, providing a quantitative reference for evaluating candidate FRUs in the following analyses.

Limitations of existing representational units

Having defined fidelity and stability, we next use these criteria to evaluate two widely studied classes of candidate FRUs: neurons and learned features Chen et al. (2025a); Huben et al. (2024); Bricken et al. (2023); Templeton et al. (2024). Neurons correspond directly to the native coordinates of internal representations, whereas learned features are obtained by decomposing these representations into latent components. For learned features, we use Gemma Scope Lieberum et al. (2024) and Llama Scope He et al. (2024), both trained on large-scale general-domain corpora (see ‘Evaluation of existing representational units’ in Methods). The results are shown in Fig. 2.

In terms of fidelity, neurons and learned features exhibit a clear contrast. Because internal representations are expressed directly in the original neuronal coordinate system, treating neurons as candidate FRUs preserves the representational information without introducing an additional approximation, making fidelity rarely a primary limitation. Learned features, by contrast, are obtained through learned decompositions of internal representations, and their reconstruction quality depends on model architecture and scale, training data and optimization settings. Pretrained learned-feature models such as Gemma Scope and Llama Scope may therefore not be fully optimized for the target representation distribution, potentially leading to information loss and lower fidelity than neurons, even when yielding more interpretable components Huben et al. (2024); Bricken et al. (2023); Templeton et al. (2024).

In terms of stability, neither neurons nor learned features fully satisfy the distinguishability required of ideal representational atoms. Neurons correspond directly to the coordinate directions of the internal representation space, but these directions need not be sufficiently distinguishable from one another. Consequently, neurons generally exhibit low stability, consistent with the widespread polysemanticity of individual neurons Olah et al. (2020). Learned features reduce representational entanglement through learned decomposition and exhibit higher stability than neurons, consistent with their greater monosemanticity Bricken et al. (2023); Templeton et al. (2024). However, their stability remains substantially below the ideal regime.

Overall, neurons and learned features exhibit distinct limitations: neurons preserve high fidelity but exhibit low stability, whereas learned features improve stability but exhibit reduced fidelity and remain below the ideal stability regime. Accordingly, neither fully satisfies the requirements of ideal representational atoms.

Threshold-activated SAEs identify representational atoms

The limitations of existing candidate FRUs raise a central question: what kind of representation learning mechanism can reliably identify representational atoms with both high fidelity and stability?

Our theoretical analysis shows that, under appropriate conditions, threshold-activated sparse autoencoders (TSAEs) can identify FRUs with both high fidelity and stability (see ‘Identification of atoms’ in Methods; Fig. 1c). We instantiate TSAEs using BiJumpReLU SAEs, which utilize learnable activation thresholds to identify representational atoms (see ‘SAE architectures’ in Methods). We evaluate their effectiveness across multiple model families, network architectures, and representation modalities, spanning diverse data distributions. We compare BiJumpReLU SAEs with several established SAE architectures Huben et al. (2024); Gao et al. (2025); Rajamanoharan et al. (2024b); Zhu et al. (2026) under the same evaluation framework. Full experimental settings are described in ‘Training details’ in Methods. Table 1 reports the main results for fidelity and stability, the two criteria used to evaluate representational atoms, with additional metrics provided in Extended Data Table 1.

Among the evaluated SAE architectures, BiJumpReLU SAEs consistently maintain high fidelity and stability across all settings, achieving the highest mean value for both metrics in all eight model–dataset combinations. TopK and AbsTopK SAEs retain relatively high fidelity but exhibit substantially lower stability, whereas ReLU SAEs achieve higher stability but generally lower fidelity. JumpReLU SAEs provide the strongest competing results in many settings, but their stability varies markedly across models, from 64.12 to 98.41. In contrast, BiJumpReLU SAEs maintain stability above 98 across all settings while further improving fidelity.

Together, these theoretical and empirical results show that TSAEs provide an effective approach for identifying representational atoms. BiJumpReLU SAEs serve as a concrete instantiation of this approach and perform consistently across diverse models, architectures, data distributions and representation modalities, providing a practical basis for identifying atoms in neural representations.

Stable atoms are more monosemantic

Monosemanticity refers to a representational unit has a consistent semantic meaning, such that its activation reliably corresponds to a specific semantic pattern Huben et al. (2024); Bricken et al. (2023); Templeton et al. (2024). Such consistency is necessary for a well-defined interpretation of the unit, as its semantic attribution otherwise remains ambiguous. Monosemanticity therefore provides a basis for analyzing the semantic organization of internal representations.

Our theoretical analysis shows that stability characterizes the distinguishability required for monorepresentationality, which constitutes a necessary structural condition for monosemanticity (see ‘Evaluation of atoms’ in Methods). However, monorepresentationality is not sufficient, because a structurally well-defined unit may still encode distinctions that do not align with human semantic categories. The relationship between stability and monosemanticity therefore requires empirical validation.

To test this relationship, we evaluate the monosemanticity of the identified FRUs and examine its association with stability (see ‘Monosemanticity evaluation details’ in Methods). Across all 40 dataset–model–SAE combinations, stability is positively correlated with monosemanticity (Spearman ρ=0.71\rho=0.71, P<0.001P<0.001; Fig. 3a). This association is preserved within each dataset, with correlations of ρ=0.74\rho=0.74 for Wikipedia, ρ=0.79\rho=0.79 for Wikidata and ρ=0.95\rho=0.95 for LAION-COCO (Fig. 3b–d). Across individual models and representation settings, all eight correlations remain positive, ranging from ρ=0.37\rho=0.37 to 0.930.93 (Fig. 3e–l). Architecture-stratified correlations and monosemanticity distributions across SAE architectures are reported in Extended Data Figs. 1 and 2. Together, these results show that greater stability is consistently associated with greater monosemanticity across model families, representation modalities and SAE architectures.

Atoms compositionally encode sememe structures

Having shown that representational atoms identified by BiJumpReLU SAEs exhibit higher stability and greater monosemanticity, we next examine how these atoms relate to human conceptual structure. Monosemanticity captures the consistency of an FRU’s semantic interpretation, but does not determine whether that FRU alone captures a complete human semantic concept. We therefore investigate whether higher-order semantic structures are encoded by single atoms or by their compositions.

We use HowNet Qi et al. (2019); Dong and Dong (2003), an expert-annotated knowledge base in which concepts are described by fine-grained semantic units called sememes. We extract internal representations of HowNet entities across layers from multiple models and identify corresponding representational atoms using BiJumpReLU SAEs (see ‘Representation extraction for cross-layer semantic alignment’ in Methods). These SAEs maintain high fidelity and stability across the evaluated models and layers (Extended Data Table 4). For each sememe, we identify the single atom with the highest set-matching F1 score across layers, where F1 summarizes the precision and recall of the atom–sememe match, and then search for the cross-layer atom combination that maximizes the same score (see ‘Semantic alignment evaluation details’ in Methods).

As shown in Fig. 4, near one-to-one correspondences between sememes and atoms are rare. Although some sememes can be recovered almost completely by a single atom, with F1 reaching 1 (Fig. 4a), such cases account for only approximately 1% of all sememes (Fig. 4b). Most sememes require multiple atoms, with the majority involving more than six atoms across all three models (Fig. 4b). These atom combinations achieve substantially higher semantic alignment (F1) than the corresponding best single atoms (Fig. 4c), primarily through higher recall without sacrificing precision (Extended Data Table 3). The number of selected atoms also increases systematically with sememe complexity, measured by the number of associated entities (Fig. 4d). These results suggest that representational atoms generally function as finer-grained semantic components whose compositions encode higher-order human semantic structures.

To determine whether this compositional advantage could arise from the cross-layer search procedure, we examine the association between cross-layer width and final F1. The Pearson correlation between them is close to zero, and the equivalence test Lakens (2017) confirms that it falls within the prespecified bound of |r|<0.10|r|<0.10 (P<0.001P<0.001; Fig. 5), indicating no practically meaningful association. Final F1 therefore does not increase systematically with cross-layer width, supporting the interpretation that the advantage of atom combinations reflects compositional structure in the internal representations rather than the search procedure.

Case-study analysis further reveals discrepancies between the entity sets recovered by atom combinations and the corresponding HowNet annotations (Extended Data Table 5; see ‘Sememe evaluation details’ in Methods). Manual inspection identifies unannotated entities that are consistent with the target sememes, as well as annotated entities that appear inconsistent with them. These cases suggest that some apparent mismatches may reflect incomplete or inaccurate annotations. Together, these findings show that single atoms capture finer-grained semantic components, while their compositions recover higher-order semantic organization that closely corresponds to human conceptual structure.

Discussion

This study focuses on a fundamental question concerning the basic units that constitute internal representations of neural networks and how their organization relates to human conceptual structure. We formulate this problem in terms of the definition, evaluation, and identification of fundamental representational units (FRUs). Drawing on compressed sensing Donoho (2006); Candès et al. (2006), we define FRUs as representational atoms and introduce fidelity and stability to characterize information preservation and structural distinguishability. We further show that threshold-activated sparse autoencoders (TSAEs) can identify such atoms under appropriate conditions, instantiate TSAEs as BiJumpReLU SAEs in practice, and validate their effectiveness across diverse models and representation settings. Further analysis indicates that more stable atoms also exhibit greater empirical monosemanticity, and their cross-layer compositions recover higher-order semantic organization corresponding to human conceptual structure. Together, these findings provide a unified theoretical and practical framework for characterizing the basic organization of neural representations and its relationship to human conceptual structure.

This framework provides a principled view of commonly studied representational units. Neurons and learned features can be evaluated within the same theoretical setting through fidelity and stability, rather than being treated solely as empirical units of interpretation. More broadly, the framework connects two influential perspectives on neural representation: the linear representation hypothesis Park et al. (2023), in which semantic information is encoded along specific directions, and the superposition hypothesis Elhage et al. (2022), which explains how finite-dimensional spaces can support substantially more linear components than their dimensionality. Their combination within a sparse linear framework provides a unified account of how representational components can remain both expressive and distinguishable.

The compositional organization of representational atoms also has implications for interventions on internal representations, including knowledge editing Meng et al. (2022); Meng et al. (2023); Hu et al. (2024) and representation steering Rimsky et al. (2024); Rodriguez et al. (2025). Such methods often rely on mapping human-defined target concepts to localizable representational structures. Our results suggest that these correspondences are often mediated by finer-grained representational atoms and their combinations, which jointly form higher-order semantic structures. Intervening on a single direction or localized representation may therefore affect only part of a target concept or simultaneously perturb multiple overlapping semantic components. This perspective may help explain incomplete edits, collateral effects and instability, and suggests that future intervention methods should explicitly consider the compositional and superpositional organization of FRUs.

This representational perspective is also relevant to continual learning Kirkpatrick et al. (2017); Van de Ven et al. (2022). Continual learning modifies internal representations through parameter updates, and superposition implies that changes to representations may perturb multiple overlapping components and thereby affect existing knowledge. This provides a possible structural account of catastrophic forgetting and suggests that robust continual learning may therefore benefit from explicitly considering the superpositional organization of FRUs. More broadly, this framework provides a basis for studying how models integrate new information while preserving previously encoded knowledge.

A natural question is whether this framework generalizes across diverse neural networks and internal representations. Its generality ultimately depends on whether stable and semantically meaningful representational atoms emerge across different models and representation spaces. Importantly, fidelity and stability provide quantitative criteria for assessing this applicability without assuming it a priori. Across the models and representation settings examined here, we observe consistent evidence for representational atoms, supporting their use as a testable and extensible basis for studying neural representations and their semantic organization.

Methods

Representational atoms theoretical framework

In neural networks, all information is embedded in high-dimensional representations. Our objective is to identify the fundamental representational units (FRUs), which we term representational atoms, or atoms for brevity. Formally, we consider a collection of representations M={𝒎i}i=1|M|M=\{\boldsymbol{m}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{|M|}, where 𝒎i∈ℝH\boldsymbol{m}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{H}. Each representation can be expressed as 𝒎i=∑jδ⁡(i,j)​𝒅j\boldsymbol{m}_{i}=\sum_{j}\delta(i,j)\boldsymbol{d}_{j}, where δ⁡(i,j)\delta(i,j) denotes the presence and magnitude of the jj-th representational unit 𝒅j∈ℝH\boldsymbol{d}_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{H} in the ii-th representation 𝒎i\boldsymbol{m}_{i}. However, in representation space, the family of representational units admitting such a decomposition is, in principle, infinite.

The central question is how to define FRUs. A natural criterion is distinguishability: each atom should be detectable or manipulable without interfering with others. In high-dimensional spaces, this criterion translates into orthogonality: atoms occupy mutually orthogonal directions, making their identities distinguishable via inner products. This motivates introducing an inner product to analyze the geometry of FRUs.

Thus, the choice of inner product is critical. Although the Euclidean inner product is commonly used, it is not necessarily appropriate for characterizing the intrinsic geometry of neural representation spaces Park et al. (2023); Hu et al. (2025). To illustrate this point, let 𝒉∈ℝH\boldsymbol{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{H} denote the internal representation at a given layer and fdownf_{\mathrm{down}} the subsequent network mapping, so that the downstream computation is 𝒚=fdown​(𝒉)\boldsymbol{y}=f_{\mathrm{down}}(\boldsymbol{h}). Because our analysis concerns the linear structure and its geometry in the representation space, we consider reparameterizations that preserve this linear structure. In a finite-dimensional real vector space, such reparameterizations are exactly invertible linear transformations, so that any bijection that preserves linearity can be uniquely written as 𝒉′=𝑨​𝒉\boldsymbol{h}^{\prime}=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{h}, where 𝑨∈ℝH×H\boldsymbol{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times H} is invertible. Accordingly, for any invertible linear transformation 𝑨\boldsymbol{A}, we can introduce the following reparameterization:

fdown′​(𝒛)←fdown​(𝑨−1​𝒛),𝒉′←𝑨​𝒉.f^{\prime}_{\mathrm{down}}(\boldsymbol{z})\leftarrow f_{\mathrm{down}}(\boldsymbol{A}^{-1}\boldsymbol{z}),\quad\boldsymbol{h}^{\prime}\leftarrow\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{h}. (4)

Then it follows that fdown′​(𝒉′)=fdown​(𝒉)f^{\prime}_{\mathrm{down}}(\boldsymbol{h}^{\prime})=f_{\mathrm{down}}(\boldsymbol{h}), leaving the input–output function unchanged. The results of Park et al. Park et al. (2023) and Hu et al. Hu et al. (2025) can be viewed as specific instances of this reparameterization principle under particular model parameterizations.

Since the above reparameterization leaves the network input–output function unchanged, 𝒉\boldsymbol{h} and 𝒉′=𝑨​𝒉\boldsymbol{h}^{\prime}=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{h} are indistinguishable from the perspective of observable network behavior. Thus, even for a fully trained network with a fixed input–output function, internal representations are identifiable only up to the equivalence class induced by invertible linear transformations 𝑨\boldsymbol{A}, rather than by unique coordinate representations determined by the network itself. By linearity, this non-uniqueness extends to the corresponding representational units 𝒅j\boldsymbol{d}_{j}. Under transformation 𝒅j′=𝑨​𝒅j\boldsymbol{d}^{\prime}_{j}=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{d}_{j}, the transformed units describe an equivalent representational structure associated with the same network function.

This has direct consequences for the geometry of the representation space. In particular, the Euclidean inner product is not invariant under the reparameterization in equation (4): ⟨𝒅i,𝒅j⟩≠⟨𝑨​𝒅i,𝑨​𝒅j⟩\langle\boldsymbol{d}_{i},\boldsymbol{d}_{j}\rangle\neq\langle\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{d}_{i},\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{d}_{j}\rangle. Therefore, geometric relations induced by the Euclidean inner product, such as angles and orthogonality, between 𝒅i\boldsymbol{d}_{i} and 𝒅j\boldsymbol{d}_{j} depend on the chosen parameterization. Thus, the Euclidean inner product does not provide a canonical geometry of neural representations that is independent of the chosen parameterization.

Atomic inner product

To better understand neural representations and thereby define atoms within them, we require additional principles to specify an appropriate inner product. We therefore introduce an inner product with the desired properties.

Definition 1 (Atomic inner product; AIP).

Let 𝒟=span⁡(D)\mathcal{D}\!=\!\mathrm{span}(D), where D={𝐝j}j=1|D|D\!=\!\{\boldsymbol{d}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{|D|} denotes the atom set. The atomic inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩S\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{S} is an inner product on 𝒟\mathcal{D} such that ⟨𝐝i,𝐝j⟩S=0\langle\boldsymbol{d}_{i},\boldsymbol{d}_{j}\rangle_{S}\!=\!0 for all 𝐝i,𝐝j∈D\boldsymbol{d}_{i},\boldsymbol{d}_{j}\in D with i≠ji\neq j.

Atoms are indexed arbitrarily, and any permutation of indices leaves their geometry invariant. Hence, there is no principled basis for assigning different norms to different atoms. By this symmetry, we assume a common norm under the chosen inner product, i.e. ‖𝒅i‖S=c>0\|\boldsymbol{d}_{i}\|_{S}\!=\!c>0, ∀i∈[|D|]\forall i\in[|D|]. The constant cc cancels naturally in subsequent analysis.

By abuse of notation, we also use 𝑫∈ℝH×|D|\boldsymbol{D}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times|D|} to denote the matrix with columns 𝒅j\boldsymbol{d}_{j}. We next characterize the atomic inner product in an explicit form.

Theorem 2 (Explicit form of the atomic inner product).

Let ⟨𝐝i,𝐝j⟩S=𝐝i⊤​𝐒​𝐝j\langle\boldsymbol{d}_{i},\boldsymbol{d}_{j}\rangle_{S}=\boldsymbol{d}_{i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{S}\boldsymbol{d}_{j} be an atomic inner product with 𝐒∈ℝH×H\boldsymbol{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times H} symmetric and positive definite. If the columns of 𝐃=[𝐝1,𝐝2,⋯,𝐝|D|]\boldsymbol{D}=[\boldsymbol{d}_{1},\boldsymbol{d}_{2},\cdots,\boldsymbol{d}_{|D|}] form the atom set such that ∀i,‖𝐝i‖S=c>0\forall i,\ \|\boldsymbol{d}_{i}\|_{S}=c>0, and 𝒟≃ℝH\mathcal{D}\simeq\mathbb{R}^{H}, then 𝐒=c2​(𝐃​𝐃⊤)−1\boldsymbol{S}=c^{2}(\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{D}^{\top})^{-1}.

All proofs are provided in the ‘Proofs’ section of the Supplementary Information. By analogy to cosine similarity, we introduce the normalized atomic inner product to remove the dependence on cc.

Corollary 3 (Normalized atomic inner product; NAIP).

Let the atomic inner product be defined by ⟨𝐝i,𝐝j⟩S=𝐝i⊤​𝐒​𝐝j\langle\boldsymbol{d}_{i},\boldsymbol{d}_{j}\rangle_{S}=\boldsymbol{d}_{i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{S}\boldsymbol{d}_{j}, where 𝐒\boldsymbol{S} is symmetric and positive definite. Suppose the columns of 𝐃=[𝐝1,⋯,𝐝|D|]\boldsymbol{D}=[\boldsymbol{d}_{1},\cdots,\boldsymbol{d}_{|D|}] form the atom set satisfying ∀i,‖𝐝i‖S=c>0\forall i,\ \|\boldsymbol{d}_{i}\|_{S}=c>0. Then, for any i,ji,j,

⟨𝒅i,𝒅j⟩S~:=⟨𝒅i,𝒅j⟩S‖𝒅i‖S​‖𝒅j‖S=𝒅i⊤​𝑺~​𝒅j,𝑺~=(𝑫​𝑫⊤)−1.\langle\boldsymbol{d}_{i},\boldsymbol{d}_{j}\rangle_{\tilde{S}}:=\frac{\langle\boldsymbol{d}_{i},\boldsymbol{d}_{j}\rangle_{S}}{\|\boldsymbol{d}_{i}\|_{S}\|\boldsymbol{d}_{j}\|_{S}}=\boldsymbol{d}_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\boldsymbol{S}}\boldsymbol{d}_{j},\quad\tilde{\boldsymbol{S}}=(\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{D}^{\top})^{-1}. (5)

Consequently, the bilinear form ⟨𝐝i,𝐝j⟩S~=𝐝i⊤​𝐒~​𝐝j\langle\boldsymbol{d}_{i},\boldsymbol{d}_{j}\rangle_{\tilde{S}}=\boldsymbol{d}_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\boldsymbol{S}}\boldsymbol{d}_{j} defines the normalized atomic inner product.

Unlike the causal inner product (Park et al., 2023), which is defined in the static and input-independent unembedding space over the output tokens, our AIP (or NAIP) operates in the dynamic and input-dependent representation space, characterizing the geometry of representations and their constituent units. This enables direct analysis of internal representations and thereby allows the definition of atoms as fundamental representational units under the AIP.

Remark.

Define 𝐝i~=𝐒~12​𝐝i\tilde{\boldsymbol{d}_{i}}\!=\!\tilde{\boldsymbol{S}}^{\frac{1}{2}}\boldsymbol{d}_{i} and 𝐝j~=𝐒~12​𝐝j\tilde{\boldsymbol{d}_{j}}\!=\!\tilde{\boldsymbol{S}}^{\frac{1}{2}}\boldsymbol{d}_{j}. Under this transformation, ⟨𝐝i,𝐝j⟩S~=⟨𝐝i~,𝐝j~⟩\langle\boldsymbol{d}_{i},\boldsymbol{d}_{j}\rangle_{\tilde{S}}=\langle\tilde{\boldsymbol{d}_{i}},\tilde{\boldsymbol{d}_{j}}\rangle, where the right-hand side denotes the Euclidean inner product. Hence, properties of the Euclidean inner product are transferred directly to the NAIP. Consequently, 𝐝i~\tilde{\boldsymbol{d}_{i}} and 𝐝j~\tilde{\boldsymbol{d}_{j}} are termed normalized atoms.

Formal definition of atoms

Having established a principled perspective for understanding neural representations, we proceed to formally define atoms. However, the preceding analysis assumes an idealized setting in which atoms are strictly orthogonal under the chosen inner product. Although this assumption yields a clean notion, it constrains the number of atoms to at most the representation dimension (|D|=H|D|=H), rendering the formulation impractical.

Elhage et al. Elhage et al. (2022) observed that sparsity induces the emergence of approximately orthogonal representations in neural networks to cope with limited representational dimensionality, a phenomenon termed superposition. Hu et al. Hu et al. (2025) later identified pervasive superposition in neural networks. Motivated by these findings, we introduce sparsity, which naturally leads to approximate orthogonality and enables a formally grounded, practical definition of atoms.

Definition 4 (Sparsity level).

Let M={𝐦i}i=1|M|⊂ℝHM\!=\!\{\boldsymbol{m}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{|M|}\!\subset\!\mathbb{R}^{H} be a collection of representations. Suppose there exist 𝐃=[𝐝1,⋯,𝐝|D|]∈ℝH×|D|\boldsymbol{D}\!=\![\boldsymbol{d}_{1},\!\cdots\!,\boldsymbol{d}_{|D|}]\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{H\times|D|} and 𝛅i∈ℝ≥0|D|\boldsymbol{\delta}_{i}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{|D|}_{\geq 0} such that 𝐦i=𝐃​𝛅i\boldsymbol{m}_{i}\!=\!\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{\delta}_{i}, ∀i∈[|M|]\forall i\!\in\![|M|]. The sparsity level is K:=maxi⁡‖𝛅i‖0K\!:=\!\max_{i}\|\boldsymbol{\delta}_{i}\|_{0}, where ∥⋅∥0\|\cdot\|_{0} denotes the ℓ0\ell_{0} norm.

Sparsity enables the number of atoms to substantially exceed the ambient dimension, yielding an overcomplete structure with |D|≫H|D|\gg H that captures rich world knowledge, while simultaneously minimizing mutual interference.

Remark.

In the basic setting described in the ‘Atomic inner product’ subsection, with |D|=H|D|=H, one can verify that 𝐒~=(𝐃​𝐃⊤)−1\tilde{\boldsymbol{S}}=(\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{D}^{\top})^{-1} satisfies 𝐃⊤​𝐒~​𝐃=𝐈|D|\boldsymbol{D}^{\top}\tilde{\boldsymbol{S}}\boldsymbol{D}=\boldsymbol{I}_{|D|}, so the atoms form an orthonormal basis under ⟨⋅,⋅⟩S\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{S}. When |D|≫H|D|\!\gg\!H, 𝐒~=(𝐃​𝐃⊤)−1\tilde{\boldsymbol{S}}\!=(\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{D}^{\top})^{-1} is well defined provided rank⁡(𝐃)=H\mathrm{rank}(\boldsymbol{D})=H, but 𝐆:=𝐃⊤​𝐒~​𝐃\boldsymbol{G}\!:=\boldsymbol{D}^{\top}\tilde{\boldsymbol{S}}\boldsymbol{D} becomes a rank-HH projection rather than 𝐈|D|\boldsymbol{I}_{|D|}, thus the atoms cannot all be mutually orthogonal under ⟨⋅,⋅⟩S\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{S}. Therefore, exact orthogonality is unattainable, motivating the introduction of approximate orthogonality.

This consideration motivates the following definition.

Definition 5 (ϵ\epsilon-Approximately Orthogonal Atoms).

The atom set {𝐝i}i=1|D|\{\boldsymbol{d}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{|D|} is ϵ\epsilon-approximately orthogonal if |⟨𝐝i,𝐝j⟩S~|≤ϵ,∀i≠j,\bigl|\langle\boldsymbol{d}_{i},\boldsymbol{d}_{j}\rangle_{\tilde{S}}\bigr|\leq\epsilon,\ \forall i\neq j, where ⟨𝐱,𝐲⟩S~:=𝐱⊤​𝐒~​𝐲\langle\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\rangle_{\tilde{S}}:=\boldsymbol{x}^{\top}\tilde{\boldsymbol{S}}\boldsymbol{y} denotes the normalized atomic inner product and 𝐒~:=(𝐃​𝐃⊤)−1\tilde{\boldsymbol{S}}:=(\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{D}^{\top})^{-1}.

Remark.

In the ideal setting of exact orthogonality, the inner products ⟨𝐝i,𝐝j⟩S~\langle\boldsymbol{d}_{i},\boldsymbol{d}_{j}\rangle_{\tilde{S}} (equivalently, ⟨𝐝i~,𝐝j~⟩\langle\tilde{\boldsymbol{d}_{i}},\tilde{\boldsymbol{d}_{j}}\rangle) for i≠ji\neq j follow a Dirac measure concentrated at the origin. Under ϵ\epsilon-approximate orthogonality, they are instead expected to follow a Gaussian distribution 𝒩⁡(0,s2)\mathcal{N}(0,s^{2}) with small variance, which converges to the Dirac measure as s→0s\to 0.

We now introduce a formal definition of atoms.

Definition 6 (Atoms).

Let M={𝐦i}i=1|M|M=\{\boldsymbol{m}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{|M|} be a collection of representations. Suppose there exists 𝐃=[𝐝1,⋯,𝐝|D|]∈ℝH×|D|\boldsymbol{D}\!=\![\boldsymbol{d}_{1},\!\cdots,\!\boldsymbol{d}_{|D|}]\!\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times|D|} and 𝚫=[𝛅1,⋯,𝛅|M|]∈ℝ≥0|D|×|M|\boldsymbol{\Delta}\!=\![\boldsymbol{\delta}_{1},\!\cdots\!,\boldsymbol{\delta}_{|M|}]\!\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{|D|\times|M|} such that, for a given sparsity level K∈ℕ+K\in\mathbb{N}^{+},

∀i∈[|M|],𝒎i=𝑫​𝜹i​ with ​‖𝜹i‖0≤K.\forall i\in[|M|],\quad\boldsymbol{m}_{i}=\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{\delta}_{i}\ \text{ with }\ \|\boldsymbol{\delta}_{i}\|_{0}\leq K. (6)

Furthermore, |⟨𝐝i,𝐝j⟩S~|≤ϵ,∀i≠j\bigl|\langle\boldsymbol{d}_{i},\boldsymbol{d}_{j}\rangle_{\tilde{S}}\bigr|\!\leq\!\epsilon,\ \forall i\!\neq\!j, where 𝐒~:=(𝐃​𝐃⊤)−1\tilde{\boldsymbol{S}}\!:=\!(\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{D}^{\top})^{-1}. Under these conditions, {𝐝i}i=1|D|\{\boldsymbol{d}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{|D|} is called the atom set of MM, and each 𝐝i\boldsymbol{d}_{i} is referred to as an atom.

Intuitively, atoms are characterized by three properties: representability, where each representation can be faithfully expressed by atoms, i.e., 𝒎i=𝑫​𝜹i\boldsymbol{m}_{i}=\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{\delta}_{i}; sparsity, where each representation involves only a few atoms, i.e., ‖𝜹i‖0≤K\|\boldsymbol{\delta}_{i}\|_{0}\leq K; and separability, where atoms are approximately orthogonal, i.e., |⟨𝒅i~,𝒅j~⟩|≤ϵ|\langle\tilde{\boldsymbol{d}_{i}},\tilde{\boldsymbol{d}_{j}}\rangle|\leq\epsilon. Representability is a natural requirement, while sparsity and separability jointly enable efficient encoding of separable information under approximate orthogonality. We further quantitatively characterize the relationship between sparsity and separability in the following ‘Evaluation of atoms’ subsection.

Remark.

KK quantifies sparsity without enforcing a specific sparsity regime, ensuring broad applicability of the definition. Moreover, pre-multiplying both sides of equation (6) by 𝐒~12\tilde{\boldsymbol{S}}^{\frac{1}{2}} yields 𝐦~i=𝐃~​𝛅i\tilde{\boldsymbol{m}}_{i}=\tilde{\boldsymbol{D}}\boldsymbol{\delta}_{i}, with 𝐦~i:=𝐒~12​𝐦i\tilde{\boldsymbol{m}}_{i}:=\tilde{\boldsymbol{S}}^{\frac{1}{2}}\boldsymbol{m}_{i} and 𝐃~:=𝐒~12​𝐃=[𝐝~1,⋯,𝐝~|D|]\tilde{\boldsymbol{D}}:=\tilde{\boldsymbol{S}}^{\frac{1}{2}}\boldsymbol{D}=[\tilde{\boldsymbol{d}}_{1},\cdots,\tilde{\boldsymbol{d}}_{|D|}], which simplifies subsequent derivations.

Evaluation of atoms

Having formalized atoms via representability, sparsity, and separability, we now evaluate whether candidate representational units satisfy the criteria of ideal atoms. Representability is measured by the coefficient of determination R2:=−∑i‖𝒙i−𝒙^i‖2∑i‖𝒙i−𝒙¯‖2R^{2}\!:=\!1\!-\!\frac{\sum_{i}\|\boldsymbol{x}_{i}-\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}_{i}\|^{2}}{\sum_{i}\|\boldsymbol{x}_{i}-\bar{\boldsymbol{x}}\|^{2}}, which quantifies the proportion of variance in the original representations explained by atoms and thus reflects fidelity. While sparsity and separability can be quantified by KK and ϵ\epsilon, they do not directly indicate unit quality. In this section, we introduce a unified metric that integrates sparsity and separability to characterize the stability of representational units.

We note that 𝜹i∈ℝ|D|\boldsymbol{\delta}_{i}\!\in\mathbb{R}^{|D|} can be viewed as a sparse representation of high-dimensional semantics, which is compressed by 𝑫∈ℝH×|D|\boldsymbol{D}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{H\times|D|} to produce 𝒎i∈ℝH\boldsymbol{m}_{i}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{H}. This perspective reveals a close connection to compressed sensing Donoho (2006); Candès et al. (2006), whose core idea is that a signal sparse in some basis can be recovered from far fewer linear measurements than its ambient dimension, with the Restricted Isometry Property (RIP) Goeßmann and Kutyniok (2020); Chen and Schaeffer (2021) providing the essential guarantee.

Definition 7 (Restricted Isometry Property; RIP).

A matrix 𝐃~∈ℝH×|D|\tilde{\boldsymbol{D}}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times|D|} is said to satisfy the KK-RIP if there exists a constant δK∈[0,1)\delta_{K}\in[0,1) such that, for any KK-sparse vector 𝛅∈ℝ|D|\boldsymbol{\delta}\in\mathbb{R}^{|D|} (i.e., ‖𝛅‖0≤K\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|_{0}\leq K),

(1−δK)​‖𝜹‖22≤‖𝑫~​𝜹‖22≤(1+δK)​‖𝜹‖22.(1-\delta_{K})\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|_{2}^{2}\leq\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{D}}\boldsymbol{\delta}\|_{2}^{2}\leq(1+\delta_{K})\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|_{2}^{2}. (7)

Here, δK\delta_{K} is called the KK-RIP constant of 𝐃~\tilde{\boldsymbol{D}}.

Intuitively, projecting a sparse vector via 𝑫~\tilde{\boldsymbol{D}} to lower dimension preserves its geometric structure, ensuring the possibility of recovery. Direct verification of the RIP is NP-hard, but coherence Foucart and Rauhut (2013); Murdock and Lucey (2020) provides a computable upper bound on δk\delta_{k}.

Theorem 8 (Coherence–RIP Upper Bound).

Let 𝐃~∈ℝH×|D|\tilde{\boldsymbol{D}}\!\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times|D|} and define the coherence μ:=maxi≠j⁡|⟨𝐝i~,𝐝j~⟩|≤ε\mu\!:=\max_{i\neq j}|\langle\tilde{\boldsymbol{d}_{i}},\tilde{\boldsymbol{d}_{j}}\rangle|\leq\varepsilon. For any KK-sparse vector 𝛅∈ℝ|D|\boldsymbol{\delta}\in\mathbb{R}^{|D|} with ‖𝛅‖0≤K\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|_{0}\leq K,

(−(K−1)​μ)​‖𝜹‖22≤‖𝑫~​𝜹‖22≤(+(K−1)​μ)​‖𝜹‖22.\big(1\!-\!(K\!-\!1)\mu\big)\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|_{2}^{2}\leq\!\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{D}}\boldsymbol{\delta}\|_{2}^{2}\!\leq\!\big(1\!+\!(K\!-\!1)\mu\big)\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|_{2}^{2}. (8)

Hence δK​(𝐃~)≤(K−1)​μ\delta_{K}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{D}})\leq(K-1)\mu. In particular, 𝐃~\tilde{\boldsymbol{D}} satisfies the KK-RIP whenever (K−1)​μ<1(K-1)\mu<1.

In other words, coherence provides a computable criterion for verifying the RIP, ensuring that all KK-sparse vectors projected through 𝑫~\tilde{\boldsymbol{D}} preserve geometric structure, an essential prerequisite in compressed sensing. Nevertheless, the RIP alone does not preclude non-uniqueness Donoho and Huo (2001); Candes and Tao (2005): even if (K−1)​μ<1(K-1)\mu<1 holds, the sparse coefficients associated with representations need not be unique.

Theorem 9 (Uniqueness and Exact ℓ1\ell_{1}\! Recoverability).

Let 𝐃~∈ℝH×|D|\tilde{\boldsymbol{D}}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times|D|} and define the coherence μ:=maxi≠j⁡|⟨𝐝i~,𝐝j~⟩|≤ε\mu:=\max_{i\neq j}|\langle\tilde{\boldsymbol{d}_{i}},\tilde{\boldsymbol{d}_{j}}\rangle|\leq\varepsilon. If μ<12​K−1\mu<\frac{1}{2K-1}, then for every 𝛅∈ℝ|D|\boldsymbol{\delta}\in\mathbb{R}^{|D|} with ‖𝛅‖0≤K\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|_{0}\leq K, the KK-sparse representation determined by 𝐦~=𝐃~​𝛅\tilde{\boldsymbol{m}}=\tilde{\boldsymbol{D}}\boldsymbol{\delta} is unique; that is, no other KK-sparse vector yields the same 𝐦~\tilde{\boldsymbol{m}}. Moreover, 𝛅\boldsymbol{\delta} is the unique minimizer of the convex program

min𝒙∈ℝ|D|⁡‖𝒙‖1subject to𝑫~​𝒙=𝒎~.\min_{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{|D|}}\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_{1}\quad\text{subject to}\quad\tilde{\boldsymbol{D}}\,\boldsymbol{x}=\tilde{\boldsymbol{m}}. (9)

Crucially, this intrinsically characterizes the monorepresentationality of 𝑫~\tilde{\boldsymbol{D}}: under the condition μ<12​K−1\mu<\tfrac{1}{2K-1}, any representation formed as a KK-sparse linear combination of representational units in 𝑫~\tilde{\boldsymbol{D}} has a unique sparse decomposition, with no other combination yielding the same representation.

Corollary 10 (Monorepresentationality / Injectivity).

Under the condition μ<12​K−1\mu<\tfrac{1}{2K-1} of Theorem 9, define ΣK:={𝛅∈ℝ|D|:‖𝛅‖0≤K}\Sigma_{K}:=\{\boldsymbol{\delta}\in\mathbb{R}^{|D|}:\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|_{0}\leq K\} and Φ:ΣK→ℝH\Phi:\Sigma_{K}\to\mathbb{R}^{H} by Φ⁡(𝛅):=𝐃~​𝛅\Phi(\boldsymbol{\delta}):=\tilde{\boldsymbol{D}}\boldsymbol{\delta}. Then Φ\Phi is injective on ΣK\Sigma_{K}. That is, for any 𝐱,𝐲∈ΣK\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\in\Sigma_{K}, if 𝐃~​𝐱=𝐃~​𝐲\tilde{\boldsymbol{D}}\boldsymbol{x}=\tilde{\boldsymbol{D}}\boldsymbol{y}, it follows that 𝐱=𝐲\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{y}.

Within this regime, representational units and their combinations are unambiguous in representation space, i.e., monorepresentationality. By contrast, monosemanticity Bricken et al. (2023); Templeton et al. (2024) concerns the alignment of a unit with a specific meaning, concept, or function. The former is formally provable, whereas the latter is statistical and interpretive. Monorepresentationality is a prerequisite for monosemanticity, as it provides the structural stability; otherwise, units would be non-unique and interpretation unstable. Without additional semantic anchoring or inductive assumptions, theoretical guarantees primarily concern structural stability induced by monorepresentationality, while monosemanticity must be determined empirically via further semantic alignment experiments.

Sparsity (KK) and separability (μ\mu) are thus unified by the condition μ<12​K−1\mu<\frac{1}{2K-1}, under which stability holds. More practical metrics are discussed in the following ‘Stability metrics and computation’ subsection.

Remark.

For intuition, the above result can be viewed as a generalization of the strictly orthogonal case (|D|=H|D|=H). In this setting, 𝐃~∈ℝH×H\tilde{\boldsymbol{D}}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times H} has orthogonal columns (μ=0\mu=0), i.e., 𝐃~⊤​𝐃~=𝐈\tilde{\boldsymbol{D}}^{\top}\tilde{\boldsymbol{D}}=\boldsymbol{I}. Any representation 𝐦~∈ℝH\tilde{\boldsymbol{m}}\in\mathbb{R}^{H} then admits a unique decomposition 𝛅=𝐃~⊤​𝐦~\boldsymbol{\delta}=\tilde{\boldsymbol{D}}^{\top}\tilde{\boldsymbol{m}}, satisfying 𝐦~=𝐃~​𝛅\tilde{\boldsymbol{m}}=\tilde{\boldsymbol{D}}\boldsymbol{\delta}. Here the sparsity level K=H=|D|K=H=|D| satisfies μ<12​K−1\mu<\tfrac{1}{2K-1}. Thus, under strict orthogonality, representations and atom coefficients are in one-to-one correspondence, yielding a direct and unique identification of atoms.

Identification of atoms

We have defined atoms and established criteria for ideal atoms. A central question remains whether such atoms can be identified in practice. Since sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a standard approach for learning disentangled representations Huben et al. (2024), we next demonstrate that, under appropriate conditions, SAEs can indeed identify these atoms, rendering the theory practically applicable.

Theorem 11 (Identifiability of Threshold-activated SAEs; TSAEs).

Let M={𝐦i}i=1|M|⊂ℝHM=\{\boldsymbol{m}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{|M|}\subset\mathbb{R}^{H} with 𝐦i=𝐃​𝛅i\boldsymbol{m}_{i}=\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{\delta}_{i}, where 𝐃=[𝐝1,⋯,𝐝|D|]∈ℝH×|D|\boldsymbol{D}=[\boldsymbol{d}_{1},\cdots,\boldsymbol{d}_{|D|}]\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times|D|} satisfies |⟨𝐝i~,𝐝j~⟩|≤ϵ|\langle\tilde{\boldsymbol{d}_{i}},\tilde{\boldsymbol{d}_{j}}\rangle|\leq\epsilon, ∀i≠j\forall i\neq j, and each 𝛅i∈ℝ|D|\boldsymbol{\delta}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{|D|} is KK-sparse, i.e. ‖𝛅i‖0≤K\|\boldsymbol{\delta}_{i}\|_{0}\leq K. Define the positive and negative supports as 𝒮i+:={j:δi​j>0},𝒮i−:={j:δi​j<0}\mathcal{S}_{i}^{+}:=\{j:\delta_{ij}>0\},\ \mathcal{S}_{i}^{-}:=\{j:\delta_{ij}<0\}, with 𝒮i=𝒮i+∪𝒮i−=supp⁡(𝛅i)\mathcal{S}_{i}=\mathcal{S}_{i}^{+}\cup\mathcal{S}_{i}^{-}=\operatorname{supp}(\boldsymbol{\delta}_{i}). Suppose there exist constants 0<δmin+≤δmax+, 0<δmin−≤δmax−0<\delta_{\min}^{+}\leq\delta_{\max}^{+},\ 0<\delta_{\min}^{-}\leq\delta_{\max}^{-}, such that δmin+≤δi​j≤δmax+,∀j∈𝒮i+\delta_{\min}^{+}\leq\delta_{ij}\leq\delta_{\max}^{+},\ \forall j\in\mathcal{S}_{i}^{+}, and −δmax−≤δi​j≤−δmin−,∀j∈𝒮i−-\delta_{\max}^{-}\leq\delta_{ij}\leq-\delta_{\min}^{-},\ \forall j\in\mathcal{S}_{i}^{-}. Consider the bidirectional threshold activation function

στ−,τ+​(x)={0,τ−≤x≤τ+,x,x<τ−​or​x>τ+,\sigma_{\tau_{-},\tau_{+}}(x)=\begin{cases}0,&\tau_{-}\leq x\leq\tau_{+},\\ x,&x<\tau_{-}\ \text{or}\ x>\tau_{+},\end{cases} (10)

with τ−<0<τ+\tau_{-}<0<\tau_{+}. Define B0:=ϵ⁡(|𝒮i+|​δmax++|𝒮i−|​δmax−)B_{0}:=\epsilon\left(|\mathcal{S}_{i}^{+}|\delta_{\max}^{+}+|\mathcal{S}_{i}^{-}|\delta_{\max}^{-}\right), B+:=ϵ⁡((|𝒮i+|−1)​δmax++|𝒮i−|​δmax−)B_{+}:=\epsilon\left((|\mathcal{S}_{i}^{+}|-1)\delta_{\max}^{+}+|\mathcal{S}_{i}^{-}|\delta_{\max}^{-}\right), and B−:=ϵ⁡(|𝒮i+|​δmax++(|𝒮i−|−1)​δmax−)B_{-}:=\epsilon\left(|\mathcal{S}_{i}^{+}|\delta_{\max}^{+}+(|\mathcal{S}_{i}^{-}|-1)\delta_{\max}^{-}\right). If the bidirectional thresholds satisfy −δmin−+B−<τ−≤−B0,B0≤τ+<δmin+−B+-\delta_{\min}^{-}+B_{-}<\tau_{-}\leq-B_{0},\ B_{0}\leq\tau_{+}<\delta_{\min}^{+}-B_{+}, with these intervals being non-empty whenever δmin−>B0+B−,δmin+>B0+B+\delta_{\min}^{-}>B_{0}+B_{-},\ \delta_{\min}^{+}>B_{0}+B_{+}, then setting the TSAE with 𝐖d​e​c=𝐃\boldsymbol{W}_{dec}=\boldsymbol{D} and 𝐖enc=𝐃⊤​𝐒~\boldsymbol{W}_{\mathrm{enc}}=\boldsymbol{D}^{\top}\tilde{\boldsymbol{S}} yields

∀i,𝑾dec​στ−,τ+​(𝑾enc​𝒎i)=𝒎i.\forall i,\quad\boldsymbol{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\,\sigma_{\tau_{-},\tau_{+}}\left(\boldsymbol{W}_{\mathrm{enc}}\boldsymbol{m}_{i}\right)=\boldsymbol{m}_{i}. (11)

This parameterization exactly recover the atom set DD.

Therefore, TSAEs can identify atoms in principle. By contrast, ReLU Huben et al. (2024), lacking a threshold term, fails to satisfy the support-separation condition and is thus theoretically insufficient. This responds to O’Neill et al. O’Neill et al. (2024): the limitation of SAEs arises not from their linear–nonlinear mechanism, but from the absence of threshold activation, which prevents effective atom identification.

The threshold activation considered here denotes a class of activation mechanisms rather than a specific instantiation. AbsTopKK Zhu et al. (2026) is formally related to this class, but relies on a prespecified KK, which limits adaptivity and practical applicability. JumpReLU Rajamanoharan et al. (2024b) and TopKK Gao et al. (2025) can also be viewed as special cases of threshold-based activation, but their one-sided activation implicitly fixes a positive orientation for each representational direction. In a general representation space, such an orientation is arbitrary, and one-sided activation may therefore introduce unnecessary dependence on the sign convention of the representational direction, whereas bidirectional threshold activation avoids this limitation.

The motivations underlying these methods are also fundamentally different. We introduce threshold activation to enable effective atom identification under approximate orthogonality. By contrast, JumpReLU Rajamanoharan et al. (2024b) was originally proposed primarily to alleviate feature shrinkage Rajamanoharan et al. (2024a), whereas TopKK was designed to control sparsity directly by retaining a fixed number of activations Gao et al. (2025). Thus, although these methods are formally related, their original objectives differ from the atom identifiability considered here.

Remark.

Although the theorem is stated for uniform scalar thresholds τ−\tau_{-} and τ+\tau_{+}, it extends directly to coordinate-wise threshold vectors 𝛕−\boldsymbol{\tau}_{-} and 𝛕+\boldsymbol{\tau}_{+} without affecting the squeeze condition or the proof. This generalization enlarges the feasible intervals when activation magnitudes vary across coordinates, thereby improving support separation and the robustness of atom identification.

Training details

To assess the applicability of the theoretical framework across model architectures and representation types, we conduct experiments on neural networks spanning multiple parameter scales, architectures and generative modalities. In the following section, we describe the extraction of internal representations and the implementation and optimization settings used to train the corresponding SAE variants.

Models and representation extraction

To cover diverse model architectures and generative paradigms, we consider Transformer-based language models (Gemma-2-2B, Gemma-2-9B Team et al. (2024), Llama-3.1-8B Grattafiori et al. (2024) and Qwen-3.5-9B Team (2026)), the hybrid-architecture language model Olmo-Hybrid-7B Merrill et al. (2026), and diffusion models (Stable Diffusion v1.5 Rombach et al. (2022) and FLUX.2-klein-9B Labs (2025)). We further cover multiple input and representation types using Wikipedia Völkel et al. (2006) for continuous-text representations, Wikidata Vrandečić and Krötzsch (2014) for discrete-entity representations, LAION-COCO Christoph et al. (2022) for representations arising during image generation, and OpenHowNet Qi et al. (2019) entity–sememe annotations for analyzing alignment between neural representational structure and human conceptual structure.

Representation extraction for SAE benchmarking

To compare BiJumpReLU SAEs with alternative SAE architectures, we select representative layers or inference stages at approximately uniform intervals and train each SAE independently on the corresponding internal representations. For language models, we follow common settings in prior representation-analysis studies Lieberum et al. (2024); He et al. (2024) and sample layers uniformly over model depth. Specifically, for Gemma-2-2B (26 layers), we use l∈{0,5,10,15,20,25}l\in\{0,5,10,15,20,25\}, and for Gemma-2-9B (42 layers), l∈{0,8,16,24,32,40}l\in\{0,8,16,24,32,40\}, extracting the output at the location ‘post_feedforward_layernorm‘. For Qwen-3.5-9B and Olmo-Hybrid-7B (both 32 layers), we use l∈{0,6,12,18,24,30}l\in\{0,6,12,18,24,30\} and extract the output at ‘down_proj‘. For diffusion models, we follow common settings from prior representation-analysis work Tinaz et al. (2025). For Stable Diffusion v1.5, we extract the output of ‘unet.mid_block.attentions‘ at normalized diffusion times t∈{0.0,0.5,1.0}t\in\{0.0,0.5,1.0\}. For FLUX.2-klein-9B, we extract the raw image-token block output from the global ‘transformer_blocks‘ at layers l∈{5,15,30}l\in\{5,15,30\} and inference steps s∈{0,3}s\in\{0,3\}. All internal representations are extracted directly from the original forward passes of the models without modifying the underlying computation and are used as input for subsequent SAE training.

Following prior empirical guidance on matching SAE capacity to representation scale Hu et al. (2026), we choose dataset sizes to maintain this balance while remaining compatible with the largest SAE configurations that can be trained reliably on a single A100 80-GB GPU. For continuous-text representations, we use Wikipedia and extract 300K internal representations at each of six representative layers for Gemma-2-2B, Gemma-2-9B, and Qwen3.5-9B, yielding 6×300​K=1.8​M6\times 300\text{K}=1.8\text{M} representations per model. For discrete-entity representations, we use Wikidata and extract 1.8​M1.8\text{M} representations per model for Gemma-2-2B, Gemma-2-9B and Olmo-Hybrid-7B under the same setting. For image-generation representations, we use LAION-COCO. Stable Diffusion v1.5 yields 3×(8×8)×10​K=1.92​M3\times(8\times 8)\times 10\text{K}=1.92\text{M} representations in three diffusion stages and 8×88\times 8 spatial positions. FLUX.2-klein-9B yields 2×3×(8×8)×10​K=3.84​M2\times 3\times(8\times 8)\times 10\text{K}=3.84\text{M} representations across two inference stages, three representative layers, and 8×88\times 8 spatial positions.

Representation extraction for cross-layer semantic alignment

To characterize the alignment between the neural representational structure and human conceptual structure, we extend representation extraction to all model layers and obtain internal representations for HowNet entities at each layer, enabling subsequent cross-layer atom identification and compositional analysis. We consider Gemma-2-2B, Gemma-2-9B, and Llama-3.1-8B. For Gemma-2-2B (26 layers) and Gemma-2-9B (42 layers), internal representations are extracted from the output at ‘post_feedforward_layernorm‘ in every layer l∈[0,26)l\in[0,26) and l∈[0,42)l\in[0,42), respectively. For Llama-3.1-8B (32 layers), internal representations are extracted from the output at ‘down_proj‘ in every layer l∈[0,32)l\in[0,32). BiJumpReLU SAEs are then trained and applied at each layer to obtain representational atoms for cross-layer composition analysis. HowNet provides approximately 123​K123\text{K} unique English entity entries for semantic alignment. Extracting representations across all layers yields approximately 26×123​K≈3.20​M26\times 123\text{K}\approx 3.20\text{M} internal representations for Gemma-2-2B, 42×123​K≈5.17​M42\times 123\text{K}\approx 5.17\text{M} for Gemma-2-9B and 32×123​K≈3.94​M32\times 123\text{K}\approx 3.94\text{M} for Llama-3.1-8B.

SAE architectures

An SAE can generally be written as

f:𝒙↦𝒙^=𝑾dec​σ​(𝑾enc​𝒙),f:\boldsymbol{x}\mapsto\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}=\boldsymbol{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\,\sigma(\boldsymbol{W}_{\mathrm{enc}}\boldsymbol{x}), (12)

where 𝒙∈ℝH\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{H}, 𝑾enc⊤,𝑾dec∈ℝH×D\boldsymbol{W}_{\mathrm{enc}}^{\top},\boldsymbol{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times D}, DD denotes the SAE dictionary width and σ\sigma is the activation function applied to the latent representation. Different SAE architectures are primarily distinguished by the form of σ\sigma. Cunningham et al. Rajamanoharan et al. (2024a) introduced the ReLU SAEs, for which

ReLU:σi​(𝒛)=max⁡(0,zi).\mathrm{ReLU}:\quad\sigma_{i}(\boldsymbol{z})=\max(0,z_{i}). (13)

Gao et al. Gao et al. (2025) proposed TopKK SAEs, which retain only the KK largest components of 𝒛\boldsymbol{z}, i.e.

TopK:σi(𝒛)=zi[i∈TopK(𝒛,K)],\mathrm{TopK}:\quad\sigma_{i}(\boldsymbol{z})=z_{i}\,\mathbf{1}\!\left[i\in\operatorname{TopK}(\boldsymbol{z},K)\right], (14)

where TopK⁡(𝒛,K)\operatorname{TopK}(\boldsymbol{z},K) denotes the index set of the KK largest components of 𝒛\boldsymbol{z}. Rajamanoharan et al. Rajamanoharan et al. (2024b) proposed the JumpReLU SAE, which introduces learnable thresholds θi\theta_{i} and retains only positive activations above the corresponding threshold

JumpReLU:σi(𝒛)=zi 1[zi>θi].\mathrm{JumpReLU}:\quad\sigma_{i}(\boldsymbol{z})=z_{i}\,\mathbf{1}[z_{i}>\theta_{i}]. (15)

Zhu et al. Zhu et al. (2026) proposed the AbsTopKK SAE, which selects the KK components with the largest activation magnitudes while preserving their original signs, i.e.

AbsTopK:σi(𝒛)=zi[i∈TopK(|𝒛|,K)].\mathrm{AbsTopK}:\quad\sigma_{i}(\boldsymbol{z})=z_{i}\,\mathbf{1}\!\left[i\in\operatorname{TopK}(|\boldsymbol{z}|,K)\right]. (16)

For the BiJumpReLU SAE introduced here, we construct a bidirectional threshold activation according to the theoretical conditions for representational atom identification:

BiJumpReLU:σi(𝒛)=zi 1[zi<τi−∨zi>τi+].\mathrm{BiJumpReLU}:\quad\sigma_{i}(\boldsymbol{z})=z_{i}\,\mathbf{1}[z_{i}<\tau_{i}^{-}\vee z_{i}>\tau_{i}^{+}]. (17)

This form follows from both the sign symmetry of representational directions and the theoretical requirements for atom identifiability. A representational direction and its negation have equivalent geometric status in the internal representation space and therefore should not be assigned an a priori preferred orientation. BiJumpReLU accordingly applies learnable thresholds to both positive and negative activations, allowing latent components to be selected without introducing a sign-dependent bias and aligning the architecture with the theoretical framework for representational atom identification.

Loss function

SAEs are trained by minimizing a joint reconstruction–sparsity objective (see Theorem 9 in ‘Evaluation of atoms’ subsection for the theoretical motivation):

ℒ⁡(𝒙)=‖𝒙−𝒙^‖22⏟ℒreconstruct+λ​‖σ⁡(𝒛)‖1⏟ℒsparsity,\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{x})=\underbrace{\|\boldsymbol{x}-\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}\|_{2}^{2}}_{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{reconstruct}}}+\lambda\underbrace{\|\sigma(\boldsymbol{z})\|_{1}}_{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sparsity}}}, (18)

where 𝒛=𝑾enc​𝒙\boldsymbol{z}=\boldsymbol{W}_{\mathrm{enc}}\boldsymbol{x}, σ\sigma denotes the activation function of the corresponding SAEs, and λ\lambda controls the trade-off between reconstruction and sparsity. ReLU SAEs use this objective directly. Because JumpReLU and BiJumpReLU SAEs contain learnable thresholds, we additionally use a straight-through estimator to approximate gradients through the thresholding operation during backpropagation Rajamanoharan et al. (2024a). By contrast, TopKK and AbsTopKK SAEs explicitly control activation sparsity through a prespecified KK and are therefore trained using only the reconstruction term, ℒ⁡(𝒙)=‖𝒙−𝒙^‖22\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{x})=\|\boldsymbol{x}-\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}\|_{2}^{2}.

Data preprocessing and hyperparameter selection

Internal representations can differ substantially in numerical scale across models, layers, and extraction sites, making SAE training highly sensitive to hyperparameter choices and complicating the use of a unified training configuration. We first observed on Gemma-2-2B that SAEs trained directly on raw activations were stable in shallow layers but became increasingly unstable in deeper layers, largely due to pronounced variation in activation scale across depth. Scaling each internal representation by the global standard deviation restored stable training across layers, with consistent behavior in Gemma-2-9B. For representations extracted from sites such as ‘down_proj‘, which are not normalized by ‘post_feedforward_layernorm‘, standard-deviation scaling alone did not yield sufficiently consistent numerical distributions. We therefore applied RMS normalization without learnable affine parameters, scaling each internal representation by its root mean square. This produced stable training for Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3.5-9B, Olmo-Hybrid-7B, Stable Diffusion v1.5 and FLUX.2-klein-9B. Accordingly, representations extracted from ‘post_feedforward_layernorm‘ in Gemma-2-2B and Gemma-2-9B use standard-deviation scaling, whereas representations from ‘down_proj‘ and other unnormalized sites use RMS normalization. Both operations apply only a scalar rescaling to each representation vector, preserving its direction and therefore the representational geometry considered here, and the original numerical scale can be recovered directly using the corresponding scaling factor.

The unified preprocessing yields comparable numerical scales across models, layers, and modalities, allowing all SAEs to use a common set of core hyperparameters without model- or layer-specific grid searches. BiJumpReLU SAEs use λ=5.0\lambda=5.0 in all settings, with the negative and positive thresholds initialized to −0.5-0.5 and 0.50.5, respectively. ReLU SAEs likewise use λ=5.0\lambda=5.0, whereas JumpReLU SAEs use λ=5.0\lambda=5.0 with the threshold initialized to 0.50.5. For TopKK SAEs, which control sparsity by fixing the number of active components, we follow the standard setting of Gao et al. Gao et al. (2025) with K=50K=50 and additionally evaluate K=20K=20 as a lower-sparsity baseline. AbsTopKK SAEs use K=50K=50, following the standard setting of Zhu et al.Zhu et al. (2026)

All remaining training settings are held fixed to minimize confounding from hyperparameter differences across SAE architectures. We use the learning rate of 2×10−42\times 10^{-4}, the Adam optimizer with β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9 and β2=0.999\beta_{2}=0.999, and the batch size of 4096 for all models. Increasing the batch size further did not yield measurable performance gains.

SAE Capacity

For SAE benchmarking, we compare the ability of different SAE architectures to identify representational atoms under otherwise matched training conditions, while keeping dictionary sizes comparable across base models. We therefore choose model-specific expansion factors such that dictionary widths remain within approximately 2.1​-​2.2×1052.1\text{-}2.2\times 10^{5}: 96×2304≈221​K96\times 2304\approx 221\text{K} for Gemma-2-2B, 60×3584≈215​K60\times 3584\approx 215\text{K} for Gemma-2-9B, 54×4096≈221​K54\times 4096\approx 221\text{K} for Qwen3.5-9B, and 58×3840≈223​K58\times 3840\approx 223\text{K} for Olmo-Hybrid-7B. For cross-layer semantic alignment, the objective is instead to obtain representational atoms with high fidelity and high stability, defined as R2>0.99R^{2}>0.99 and q∗>0.99q^{*}>0.99. Following the empirical guidance of Hu et al. Hu et al. (2026), we select the SAE dictionary as compact as possible that satisfies these criteria and keep its width fixed across all layers of the same base model. Specifically, we use 64×2304≈147​K64\times 2304\approx 147\text{K} for Gemma-2-2B, 40×3584≈143​K40\times 3584\approx 143\text{K} for Gemma-2-9B, and 35×4096≈143​K35\times 4096\approx 143\text{K} for Llama-3.1-8B.

Training dynamics and early stopping

SAE training is commonly viewed as a trade-off between reconstruction quality and sparsity Gao et al. (2025), but we observe a consistent training dynamic across multiple experimental settings. For BiJumpReLU SAEs, reconstruction and sparsity losses typically decrease together during early and intermediate training. As training progresses, the reconstruction loss gradually plateaus and may subsequently increase slightly but persistently, while sparsity continues to improve. Both objectives eventually reach an approximately stable regime. This pattern indicates that late-stage optimization primarily trades a limited change in reconstruction quality for increased sparsity, rather than continuing to improve both objectives simultaneously. Based on this dynamic, we adopt a trajectory-based early stopping criterion. For BiJumpReLU and JumpReLU SAEs, we smooth the training-loss curves and stop training near the transition at which reconstruction loss shifts from sustained decrease to a stable increase while sparsity continues to improve. This stage typically already corresponds to high fidelity and stability, allowing us to avoid unnecessary late-stage trade-offs while preserving atom-identification quality. For ReLU SAEs, where this transition is generally less pronounced, training is stopped when neither reconstruction nor sparsity loss shows further substantial improvement. For TopKK and AbsTopKK SAEs, whose sparsity is explicitly fixed by KK, training is stopped when the reconstruction performance no longer improves appreciably.

Evaluation details

To systematically evaluate the quality and semantic organization of identified representational atoms, we describe the implementation of fidelity and stability metrics, monosemanticity evaluation, and alignment analysis between neural representational structure and human conceptual structure in the following subsection.

Fidelity metrics and computation

Fidelity measures how well candidate FRUs preserve or reconstruct the original internal representations and is quantified by the coefficient of determination

R2:=1−∑i‖𝒎i−𝒎^i‖22∑i‖𝒎i−𝒎¯‖22,R^{2}:=1-\frac{\sum_{i}\|\boldsymbol{m}_{i}-\hat{\boldsymbol{m}}_{i}\|_{2}^{2}}{\sum_{i}\|\boldsymbol{m}_{i}-\bar{\boldsymbol{m}}\|_{2}^{2}}, (19)

where 𝒎^i\hat{\boldsymbol{m}}_{i} denotes the internal representation reconstructed from the candidate FRUs and 𝒎¯\bar{\boldsymbol{m}} is the sample mean. Values of R2R^{2} closer to 1 indicate more faithful reconstruction of the original representations.

Stability metrics and computation

To transform the distinguishability condition μ<1/(2​K−1)\mu<1/(2K-1) from Theorems 9 and Corollary 10 into a computable stability metric, we introduce quantile statistics that characterize the empirical distributions of sparsity and coherence. We first define the quantile sparsity KqK_{q} as

Kq=inf{k∈ℕ+∣ℙ𝜹∼𝒫Δ​(‖𝜹‖0≤k)≥q},K_{q}=\inf\left\{k\in\mathbb{N}^{+}\mid\mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol{\delta}\sim\mathcal{P}_{\Delta}}\bigl(\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|_{0}\leq k\bigr)\geq q\right\}, (20)

where 𝜹\boldsymbol{\delta} is sampled from the coefficient distribution 𝒫Δ\mathcal{P}_{\Delta}. Thus, KqK_{q} is the smallest integer such that at least a fraction qq of samples have sparsity no greater than KqK_{q}.

Similarly, we define the quantile coherence μq\mu_{q} as

μq=inf{μ≥0∣ℙ(ℐ,𝒥)​(|⟨𝒅~ℐ,𝒅~𝒥⟩|≤μ)≥q},\mu_{q}=\inf\left\{\mu\geq 0\mid\mathbb{P}_{(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J})}\left(\left|\left\langle\tilde{\boldsymbol{d}}_{\mathcal{I}},\tilde{\boldsymbol{d}}_{\mathcal{J}}\right\rangle\right|\leq\mu\right)\geq q\right\}, (21)

where (ℐ,𝒥)(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J}) is sampled uniformly from the unordered pairs of distinct representational-unit indices, and |⟨𝒅~ℐ,𝒅~𝒥⟩|\left|\left\langle\tilde{\boldsymbol{d}}_{\mathcal{I}},\tilde{\boldsymbol{d}}_{\mathcal{J}}\right\rangle\right| denotes their coherence. Consequently, μq\mu_{q} gives an upper bound on coherence satisfied by at least a fraction qq of unit pairs.

Using the distinguishability criterion above, we evaluate μq<12​Kq−1\mu_{q}<\frac{1}{2K_{q}-1} at each quantile and define stability as the largest quantile that satisfies the condition

q∗:=sup{q∣μq<12​Kq−1}.q^{*}:=\sup\left\{q\mid\mu_{q}<\frac{1}{2K_{q}-1}\right\}. (22)

Thus, q∗q^{*} denotes the largest quantile at which empirical sparsity and coherence satisfy the theoretical distinguishability condition, with the ideal value q∗=1q^{*}=1.

In practice, we compute q∗q^{*} using binary search. Specifically, on [0,0.999999][0,0.999999], we iteratively evaluate

μα:=Quantile⁡(μ,α),Kα:=Quantile⁡(K,α),\mu_{\alpha}:=\operatorname{Quantile}(\mu,\alpha),\quad K_{\alpha}:=\operatorname{Quantile}(K,\alpha), (23)

and test whether μα<12​Kα−1\mu_{\alpha}<\frac{1}{2K_{\alpha}-1}.If the condition is satisfied, the lower search bound increases; otherwise, the upper bound decreases until convergence. The largest feasible quantile is reported as q∗q^{*}.

Evaluation of existing representational units

To evaluate existing representational units within a unified framework, we treat neurons and learned features by publicly available SAEs as candidate FRUs and assess them using the fidelity and stability metrics defined above. All evaluations use approximately 20​K20\text{K} entities appearing in CounterFact Meng et al. (2022), which can be regarded as a subset of Wikidata entities. Each entity is converted into a corresponding prompt and fed into the model, and internal representations are extracted at the final token position of the target site. Neurons and learned features are evaluated directly using the original models and publicly released SAE checkpoints, without additional training or parameter tuning.

For neurons, we extract the input to the MLP ‘down_proj‘ at each layer. This vector corresponds to the activations of the intermediate MLP neurons, with each component indicating the activation strength of the corresponding neuron. The columns of the ‘down_proj‘ weight matrix are therefore treated as the representational directions associated with individual neurons, and the corresponding input activations as their coefficients, allowing the MLP residual update to be expressed as a linear combination of neuron directions. Fidelity and stability are then computed for neurons as candidate FRUs according to the definitions above.

For learned features, we use the pretrained SAEs provided by Gemma Scope Lieberum et al. (2024) and Llama Scope He et al. (2024), following their official settings. For Gemma-2-2B and Gemma-2-9B, we extract representations at the output of ‘post_feedforward_layernorm‘ from each layer and apply the corresponding Gemma Scope SAE. For Llama-3.1-8B, we extract representations at the output of ‘down_proj‘ from each layer and apply the corresponding Llama Scope SAE. The decoder directions of each SAE are treated as candidate FRUs, and the latent activations as their coefficients. The resulting SAE reconstructions are used to compute fidelity, whereas feature coherence and activation sparsity are used to compute stability under the same evaluation procedure.

Monosemanticity evaluation details

To evaluate the monosemanticity of the candidate FRUs, we use a common scoring criterion across language models and diffusion models, with modality-specific evaluation procedures. For language models, including Gemma-2-2B, Gemma-2-9B, Qwen3.5-9B and Olmo-Hybrid-7B, we use an LLM-as-a-judge protocol supplemented by manual verification. For diffusion models, including Stable Diffusion v1.5 and FLUX.2-klein-9B, we use manual evaluation. Both procedures follow the same definition of monosemanticity and a closely matched scoring template.

For each model and representation extraction site, we randomly sample 10 candidate FRUs identified by the corresponding SAE and collect the input instances that activate each unit. If more than 10 instances are activated, we randomly sample 10 for evaluation. The evaluated instances are contextualized tokens for Wikipedia, entities for Wikidata and local image patches for LAION-COCO. For each candidate FRU, we identify the largest subset SmaxS_{\max} of evaluated instances that can be coherently explained by a common concept, attribute or semantic pattern, and define its monosemanticity score as

Monosemanticity=|Smax||S|,\mathrm{Monosemanticity}=\frac{|S_{\max}|}{|S|}, (24)

where SS denotes the complete set of evaluated instances for that unit. Scores closer to 1 indicate that the unit activates more consistently on a coherent semantic pattern. Finally, we average the monosemanticity scores of the sampled units within each SAE setting to obtain its overall monosemanticity score.

Semantic alignment evaluation details

HowNet Qi et al. (2019) contains 2,540 sememes, each associated with a set of entities belonging to the corresponding semantic category. To ensure that subsequent set-based comparisons are meaningful, we retain only sememes containing at least two unique entities, yielding 2,135 sememes, which we use as an operational representation of human conceptual semantic structure. On the model side, we extract internal representations corresponding to HowNet entities at every layer and train BiJumpReLU SAEs at each layer to identify atoms. For each unit, we record the set of entities that activate it and likewise retain only units associated with at least two unique entities. Each retained sememe and representational unit can therefore be represented as an entity set, providing a common basis for comparing neural representational structure with human conceptual structure.

To evaluate semantic alignment between single atoms and HowNet sememes, we compute precision, recall and F1 based on the overlap between their corresponding entity sets. For each sememe, we search across all atoms identified at all layers and define the unit with the highest F1 score as its best single-unit match. This metric jointly reflects the semantic purity of a atom and its coverage of the target sememe, thereby quantifying the extent to which an single atoms corresponds to human conceptual semantic structure. Detailed set construction, metric definitions and cross-layer search procedures are provided in ‘Single-atom semantic alignment evaluation’ in the Supplementary Information.

Building on the single-atom analysis, we further assess whether combinations of atoms can recover sememe structure more completely.
